definition.text: Homeostasis is the body's maintenance of stable internal conditions, achieved largely through negative feedback — a mechanism that reverses any deviation from a set point and so keeps physiological values within their normal range.

anchor.quote: Negative feedback is a mechanism that reverses a deviation from the set point

facts.text: A set point is the physiological value around which the normal range fluctuates.

anchor.quote: A set point is the physiological value around which the normal range fluctuates

facts.text: Negative feedback keeps body parameters within their normal range.

anchor.quote: negative feedback maintains body parameters within their normal range

facts.text: A feedback loop has three parts: a sensor (receptor) that monitors the value, a control center that compares it to the normal range, and an effector that drives the correcting change.

anchor.quote: An effector is the component in a feedback system that causes a change to reverse the situation and return the value to the normal range

misconceptions.text: Students assume negative feedback means an effect that is harmful or that shuts a process down.
misconceptions.corrective: "Negative" describes the direction of the correction, not a bad outcome: the response opposes (reverses) the deviation to restore the set point — fever-breaking sweating and shivering are both negative-feedback responses.

examples.text: Body temperature: when blood warms above the set point, the hypothalamus triggers sweating and vasodilation until temperature falls back toward normal.

mcBank.stem: In a negative feedback loop, the role of the effector is to
options: produce a change that reverses the deviation
detect the original change in the value
store a memory of past deviations
set a brand-new physiological set point

mcBank.stem: Why is the temperature-regulating system described as negative feedback?
options: The response opposes the change and restores the set point
The response amplifies the original change
It always lowers body temperature
It works only when the patient is ill

mapping.system: a regulated physiological variable such as body temperature
mapping.output signal: the sensed deviation from the set point
mapping.feedback path: sensor to control center to effector
mapping.effect on input: the effector reverses the deviation back toward the set point

definition.text: The human body is organized in a hierarchy of increasing complexity — from atoms and molecules to cells, tissues, organs, organ systems, and finally the whole organism.

anchor.quote: subatomic particles, atoms, molecules, organelles, cells, tissues, organs, organ systems, organisms and biosphere

facts.text: A cell is the smallest independently functioning unit of a living organism.

anchor.quote: A cell is the smallest independently functioning unit of a living organism

facts.text: A tissue is a group of many similar cells that work together to perform a specific function.

anchor.quote: A tissue is a group of many similar cells (though sometimes composed of a few related types) that work together to perform a specific function

facts.text: An organ is an anatomically distinct structure built from two or more tissue types.

anchor.quote: An organ is an anatomically distinct structure of the body composed of two or more tissue types

facts.text: An organ system is a group of organs that work together to meet a physiological need of the body.

anchor.quote: An organ system is a group of organs that work together to perform major functions or meet physiological needs of the body

misconceptions.text: Students think an organ is just a bigger version of a tissue.
misconceptions.corrective: An organ combines two or more different tissue types into one functional structure — the stomach, for example, has epithelial, muscle, nervous, and connective tissue working together.

examples.text: The cardiovascular system (organ system) contains the heart (organ), built from cardiac muscle tissue, made of cardiomyocyte cells.

mcBank.stem: Which sequence lists the levels of organization from simplest to most complex?
options: cell, tissue, organ, organ system
organ, tissue, cell, organ system
tissue, cell, organ system, organ
organ system, organ, cell, tissue

mcBank.stem: What distinguishes an organ from a tissue?
options: An organ combines two or more tissue types
An organ is always larger than any tissue
An organ contains only one kind of cell
An organ cannot belong to an organ system

attribution: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §1.2 Structural Organization of the Human Body

definition.text: Blood is a fluid connective tissue made of a liquid extracellular matrix (plasma) and formed elements — red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets — that together transport gases and nutrients, defend the body, and regulate its chemistry.

anchor.quote: Recall that blood is a connective tissue

facts.text: Plasma is the fluid extracellular matrix that makes blood unique among connective tissues.

anchor.quote: The extracellular matrix, called plasma, makes blood unique among connective tissues because it is fluid

facts.text: The formed elements are red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets.

anchor.quote: the formed elements—include red blood cells (RBCs), white blood cells (WBCs), and cell fragments called platelets

facts.text: Blood's primary job is to deliver oxygen and nutrients to cells and carry wastes away.

anchor.quote: The primary function of blood is to deliver oxygen and nutrients to and remove wastes from body cells

facts.text: Blood also helps regulate the pH and chemical balance of body tissues.

anchor.quote: helps to regulate the pH of body tissues

misconceptions.text: Students think of blood as a simple liquid rather than a tissue.
misconceptions.corrective: Blood is a connective tissue: it has cellular formed elements suspended in an extracellular matrix (plasma), the same organization as bone or cartilage — only the matrix is fluid.

examples.text: A complete blood count (CBC) reports the formed elements — RBCs, WBCs, and platelets — that a nurse reviews when assessing a patient.

mcBank.stem: Which three groups make up the formed elements of blood?
options: Red cells, white cells, and platelets
Plasma, dissolved serum, and water proteins
Arteries, large veins, and tiny capillaries
Oxygen, food nutrients, and signaling hormones

mcBank.stem: Blood is classified as a connective tissue because it has
options: cellular elements suspended in an extracellular matrix
no cells, only dissolved gases
a rigid solid framework like bone
only one type of cell

attribution: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §18.1 An Overview of Blood

definition.text: The cardiac cycle is one complete heartbeat — from contraction of the atria through ventricular relaxation; cardiac output, the blood each ventricle pumps per minute, equals heart rate times stroke volume.

anchor.quote: ends with ventricular relaxation is known as the cardiac cycle

facts.text: Systole is the contraction phase that pumps blood into circulation.

anchor.quote: The period of contraction that the heart undergoes while it pumps blood into circulation is called systole

facts.text: Diastole is the relaxation phase during which the chambers fill with blood.

anchor.quote: The period of relaxation that occurs as the chambers fill with blood is called diastole

facts.text: Cardiac output (CO) is the amount of blood pumped by each ventricle in one minute.

anchor.quote: Cardiac output (CO) is a measurement of the amount of blood pumped by each ventricle in one minute

facts.text: Cardiac output is the product of heart rate and stroke volume: CO = HR × SV.

anchor.quote: CO = HR × SV

misconceptions.text: Students assume a fast heart rate always means a high cardiac output.
misconceptions.corrective: Output depends on both factors (CO = HR × SV): a very fast rate can shorten filling time and lower stroke volume, so cardiac output can fall even as heart rate climbs.

examples.text: A resting adult with a heart rate of 75 bpm and a stroke volume of 70 mL has a cardiac output of about 5.25 L/min.

workedExamples.problem: A resting patient has a heart rate of 75 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 70 mL. Calculate the cardiac output in liters per minute.
steps: Write the equation: CO = HR × SV.
Substitute the values: CO = 75 beats/min × 70 mL/beat = 5250 mL/min.
workedExamples.result: CO ≈ 5.25 L/min — a normal resting value.

anchor.quote: the mean CO is 5.25 L/min

mcBank.stem: A patient's heart rate is 80 bpm and stroke volume is 60 mL. What is the cardiac output?
options: 4800 mL/min
140 mL/min
1.33 mL/min
480 mL/min

mcBank.stem: During systole, the heart is
options: contracting and pumping blood into circulation
relaxing while the chambers fill
neither contracting nor filling
filling only the atria with blood

mapping.process: the cardiac cycle of one heartbeat
mapping.stages: atrial contraction, ventricular systole, ventricular diastole
mapping.dependency: ventricles must fill during diastole before they can eject during systole
mapping.failure if skipped: too little filling time lowers stroke volume and cardiac output

attribution: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §19.3 Cardiac Cycle; §19.4 Cardiac Physiology

definition.text: Blood pressure is the force blood exerts on vessel walls; it is reported as a systolic value (during ventricular contraction) over a diastolic value (during ventricular relaxation), and blood flows from higher to lower pressure against vascular resistance.

anchor.quote: blood pressure, the force exerted by blood upon the walls of the blood vessels or the chambers of the heart

facts.text: Systolic pressure (typically around 120 mm Hg) is the higher value, produced during ventricular contraction.

anchor.quote: The systolic pressure is the higher value (typically around 120 mm Hg)

facts.text: Diastolic pressure (usually about 80 mm Hg) is the lower value, present during ventricular relaxation.

anchor.quote: The diastolic pressure is the lower value (usually about 80 mm Hg)

facts.text: Blood moves from a region of higher pressure to one of lower pressure.

anchor.quote: blood moves from higher pressure to lower pressure

facts.text: Resistance to flow depends on just three variables: blood viscosity, vessel length, and vessel radius.

anchor.quote: there are only three variables: viscosity, vessel length, and radius

misconceptions.text: Students think the diastolic number reflects the heart actively pumping.
misconceptions.corrective: Diastolic pressure is measured during ventricular relaxation, when the heart is not ejecting blood — it reflects the residual arterial pressure between beats, not active pumping.

examples.text: A reading of 120/80 mm Hg gives the systolic pressure over the diastolic pressure — the standard way a nurse records a blood pressure.

mcBank.stem: In a blood pressure of 118/76 mm Hg, the value 76 represents the
options: arterial pressure during ventricular relaxation
arterial pressure during ventricular contraction
total resistance of the vessels
heart rate in beats per minute

mcBank.stem: Which factor does NOT directly determine resistance to blood flow?
options: The patient's heart rate
Blood viscosity
Vessel length
Vessel radius

attribution: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §20.2 Blood Flow, Blood Pressure, and Resistance

definition.text: Gas exchange is the diffusion of oxygen and carbon dioxide between air and blood; external respiration moves these gases between the alveoli and the pulmonary capillaries, each gas flowing from higher to lower partial pressure.

anchor.quote: External respiration is the exchange of gases with the external environment, and occurs in the alveoli of the lungs

facts.text: Internal respiration is the exchange of gases between blood and the tissues.

anchor.quote: Internal respiration is the exchange of gases with the internal environment, and occurs in the tissues

facts.text: A gas diffuses from where its partial pressure is higher to where it is lower.

anchor.quote: A gas will move from an area where its partial pressure is higher to an area where its partial pressure is lower

facts.text: In external respiration oxygen diffuses from the alveolus into the capillary while carbon dioxide diffuses out of the capillary into the alveolus.

anchor.quote: oxygen diffuses across the respiratory membrane from the alveolus to the capillary, whereas carbon dioxide diffuses out of the capillary into the alveolus

misconceptions.text: Students think the body actively pumps oxygen across the lung membrane.
misconceptions.corrective: No energy is spent moving the gas across the membrane: oxygen and carbon dioxide cross by simple diffusion down their own partial-pressure gradients, from high to low.

examples.text: Supplemental oxygen raises the partial pressure of oxygen in the alveoli, steepening the gradient so more oxygen diffuses into a hypoxic patient's blood.

mcBank.stem: Why does oxygen move from the alveoli into the pulmonary capillary blood?
options: Its partial pressure is higher in the alveoli than in the blood
The blood actively pumps it across the membrane
Carbon dioxide pushes it out of the alveoli
The lungs heat the oxygen until it expands

mcBank.stem: External respiration takes place
options: in the alveoli of the lungs
in the body's tissue cells
inside red blood cells only
in the walls of the heart

attribution: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §22.4 Gas Exchange

definition.text: Fluid and electrolyte balance is the maintenance of water and dissolved ions across the body's compartments — chiefly the intracellular fluid inside cells and the extracellular fluid around them — with water shifting by osmosis to keep them in equilibrium.

anchor.quote: The intracellular fluid (ICF) compartment is the system that includes all fluid enclosed in cells by their plasma membranes

facts.text: Adults are roughly 50–60 percent water by mass; infants are about 75 percent.

anchor.quote: ranging from about 75 percent of body mass in infants to about 50–60 percent in adults

facts.text: Extracellular fluid surrounds all the cells of the body.

anchor.quote: Extracellular fluid (ECF) surrounds all cells in the body

facts.text: An electrolyte is a mineral that has dissociated from a salt and carries an electrical charge (an ion).

anchor.quote: a mineral dissociated from a salt that carries an electrical charge (an ion) is called an electrolyte

facts.text: Water moves between the compartments by osmosis to keep them balanced.

anchor.quote: water moves by osmosis from plasma to the IF (and the reverse) and from the IF to the ICF (and the reverse)

misconceptions.text: Students think water is actively pumped from one fluid compartment to another.
misconceptions.corrective: Water itself follows osmosis passively — it moves toward the compartment with more solute; the body controls fluid shifts mainly by moving electrolytes, and water follows.

examples.text: Giving a hypertonic IV solution draws water out of cells by osmosis into the extracellular fluid — the basis for treating some cases of cerebral edema.

mcBank.stem: A substance that dissociates from a salt and carries an electrical charge is called
options: an electrolyte
an organelle
a tissue
a counterstain

mcBank.stem: How does water move between the body's fluid compartments?
options: Passively by osmosis toward higher solute concentration
By active transport requiring ATP
Only from the ICF into the ECF, never back
Only when the patient is dehydrated

mapping.system: the body's intracellular and extracellular fluid compartments
mapping.opposing processes: osmotic water movement into versus out of the cells
mapping.restoring force: osmosis shifting water until concentrations equalize

attribution: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §26.1 Body Fluids and Fluid Compartments

definition.text: Innate immunity is the body's built-in, nonspecific first response that lacks memory, while adaptive immunity is a slower, highly specific defense that targets individual pathogens and remembers them after exposure.

anchor.quote: Nonspecific innate defenses provide an immediate (or very rapid) response against potential pathogens

facts.text: Innate defenses are built-in mechanisms that are not acquired over time and have no memory.

anchor.quote: they are not acquired over time and they have no "memory"

facts.text: Innate immunity targets pathogens in a nonspecific manner.

anchor.quote: a multifaceted system of defenses that targets invading pathogens in a nonspecific manner

facts.text: Adaptive immunity is highly specific for individual microbial pathogens.

anchor.quote: an adaptive immune defense, which is highly specific for individual microbial pathogens

facts.text: Adaptive immunity is acquired through active infection or vaccination and defends against pathogens that evade innate immunity.

anchor.quote: acquired through active infection or vaccination and serves as an important defense against pathogens that evade the defenses of innate immunity

misconceptions.text: Students think the innate immune system gets stronger after repeated exposure to the same pathogen.
misconceptions.corrective: Innate defenses have no memory and do not improve with repeated exposure — it is adaptive immunity that builds memory through infection or vaccination for a faster response next time.

examples.text: A vaccine trains adaptive immunity to recognize one pathogen, whereas the skin barrier and fever respond to any invader nonspecifically.

mcBank.stem: Which feature best distinguishes adaptive immunity from innate immunity?
options: It is specific for individual pathogens
It responds within minutes to any invader
It is built in and never changes
It works without any prior exposure

mcBank.stem: Why does a second exposure to a pathogen produce a faster response?
options: Adaptive immunity formed memory of that pathogen
Innate immunity improves with each exposure
The skin barrier becomes thicker
Fever lasts longer the second time

attribution: OpenStax Microbiology, Ch. 17 Innate Nonspecific Host Defenses (intro); Ch. 18 Adaptive Specific Host Defenses (intro)

definition.text: Inflammation is the body's short-term innate response to injury or infection, marked by five cardinal signs — redness, swelling, heat, pain, and altered function — and driven by vasodilation and increased vascular permeability.

anchor.quote: Acute inflammation is a short-term inflammatory response to an injury or infection

facts.text: The five cardinal signs of inflammation are erythema (redness), edema (swelling), heat, pain, and altered function.

anchor.quote: erythema (redness), edema (swelling), heat, pain, and altered function

facts.text: Vasodilation and increased vascular permeability follow the release of histamine from mast cells.

anchor.quote: Vasodilation and increased vascular permeability, as a direct result of the release of histamine from resident mast cells

facts.text: Increased vascular permeability lets fluid, proteins, and immune cells enter the infected tissue.

anchor.quote: increased vascular permeability allows fluid, proteins, phagocytes, and other immune cells to enter infected tissue

misconceptions.text: Students view inflammation as purely harmful and always to be suppressed.
misconceptions.corrective: Inflammation is a protective innate response that delivers immune cells and dilutes toxins at the injury site; it becomes harmful mainly when it is excessive or chronic, not by its nature.

examples.text: A splinter site turns red, warm, swollen, and painful — the cardinal signs as blood flow and permeability rise to fight infection.

mcBank.stem: Which chemical mediator causes the vasodilation seen in acute inflammation?
options: Histamine released from mast cells
Crystal violet from the Gram stain
Safranin from the counterstain
Peptidoglycan from the cell wall

mcBank.stem: Increased vascular permeability during inflammation primarily allows
options: fluid and immune cells to enter the infected tissue
red blood cells to stop carrying oxygen
bacteria to leave the tissue unharmed
the heart rate to slow down

mapping.stages: tissue injury, histamine release, vasodilation and increased permeability, immune-cell influx
mapping.dependency: vasodilation and permeability must rise before fluid and cells can reach the tissue
mapping.failure if skipped: without the permeability change immune cells cannot enter the infected site

definition.text: Bacteria are distinguished by a cell wall whose main component is peptidoglycan; the Gram stain sorts them into gram-positive species with a thick peptidoglycan layer and gram-negative species with a thin layer plus an outer membrane.

anchor.quote: The major component of bacterial cell walls is called peptidoglycan (or murein); it is only found in bacteria

facts.text: Gram-positive cells have many layers of peptidoglycan, totaling 30–100 nm thick.

anchor.quote: Gram-positive cells have a cell wall consisting of many layers of peptidoglycan totaling 30–100 nm in thickness

facts.text: Gram-negative cells have a much thinner peptidoglycan layer and a more complex cell envelope.

anchor.quote: Gram-negative cells have a much thinner layer of peptidoglycan (no more than about 4 nm thick)

facts.text: Gram-positive cells retain the crystal violet dye and remain purple.

anchor.quote: they generally retain the crystal violet dye and remain purple

facts.text: Gram-negative cells lose the crystal violet and take up the pink safranin counterstain.

anchor.quote: the red, safranin-dyed cells are gram-negative

misconceptions.text: Students think the Gram stain color is just an arbitrary dye choice.
misconceptions.corrective: The color reflects real wall structure: a thick peptidoglycan layer traps crystal violet (purple, gram-positive) while a thin layer washes out and takes the safranin counterstain (pink, gram-negative).

examples.text: A Gram stain showing purple clusters points the team toward gram-positive Staphylococcus, guiding the choice of antibiotic.

mcBank.stem: A bacterium appears pink after Gram staining. This indicates it is
options: gram-negative with a thin peptidoglycan layer
gram-positive with a thick peptidoglycan layer
a virus rather than a bacterium
dead and unable to take up dye

mcBank.stem: What is the major component of the bacterial cell wall?
options: Peptidoglycan
Cholesterol
Crystal violet
Hemoglobin

mapping.boundary: the peptidoglycan cell wall and cell envelope
mapping.what crosses: nutrients and the Gram-stain dyes that probe wall thickness
mapping.what is excluded: the loss of crystal violet in thin-walled gram-negative cells

attribution: OpenStax Microbiology, §3.3 Unique Characteristics of Prokaryotic Cells; §2.4 Staining Microscopic Specimens

definition.text: Viruses are acellular parasites that cannot reproduce on their own; they replicate through an ordered cycle inside a host cell — attachment, penetration, biosynthesis, maturation, and release.

anchor.quote: All viruses depend on cells for reproduction and metabolic processes

facts.text: The five stages of the bacteriophage replication cycle are attachment, penetration, biosynthesis, maturation, and release.

anchor.quote: attachment, penetration, biosynthesis, maturation, and release

facts.text: Attachment begins when the virus interacts with specific receptors on the host cell surface.

anchor.quote: the phage interacts with specific bacterial surface receptors

facts.text: Many viruses are released when mature progeny burst the host cell in a process called lysis.

anchor.quote: Mature viruses burst out of the host cell in a process called lysis

misconceptions.text: Students think antibiotics can cure viral infections such as the common cold or influenza.
misconceptions.corrective: Antibiotics target bacterial structures like the cell wall and have no effect on viruses, which replicate inside host cells; viral illnesses need antivirals or are managed supportively, and misusing antibiotics only drives resistance.

examples.text: Influenza virus attaches to receptors on respiratory cells, hijacks them to make new virions, then releases them to infect neighboring cells.

mcBank.stem: Which is the correct order of the viral replication cycle?
options: Attachment, penetration, biosynthesis, maturation, release
Release, maturation, attachment, penetration, biosynthesis
Biosynthesis, attachment, release, penetration, maturation
Penetration, release, attachment, maturation, biosynthesis

mcBank.stem: Why are antibiotics ineffective against the influenza virus?
options: Antibiotics target bacterial structures, not viruses
Viruses are larger than bacteria
Influenza has a thick peptidoglycan wall
Antibiotics only work after vaccination

mapping.dependency: the virus must attach and penetrate before its genome can be biosynthesized
mapping.failure if skipped: blocking attachment prevents the whole cycle and stops infection

attribution: OpenStax Microbiology, §6.2 The Viral Life Cycle

definition.text: Antimicrobial resistance is a microbe's acquired ability to withstand a drug it was once susceptible to; it spreads through selection of resistant mutants and is accelerated by overuse and misuse of antimicrobials.

anchor.quote: Antimicrobial resistance is the acquired ability of a microbe to resist the effects of an antimicrobial drug to which it was previously susceptible

facts.text: Drug exposure selects for chromosomal mutations that confer resistance, which pass to later generations.

anchor.quote: select for chromosomal mutations conferring resistance, which can be transferred vertically to subsequent microbial generations

facts.text: Overuse and misuse of antimicrobials, subtherapeutic dosing, and patient noncompliance accelerate resistance.

anchor.quote: the overuse and misuse of antimicrobials, inappropriate use of antimicrobials, subtherapeutic dosing, and patient noncompliance

facts.text: Some resistance genes code for enzymes that chemically modify or destroy the drug.

anchor.quote: Resistance genes may code for enzymes that chemically modify an antimicrobial, thereby inactivating it

misconceptions.text: Patients believe stopping an antibiotic early once they feel better is harmless.
misconceptions.corrective: Stopping early is subtherapeutic dosing and patient noncompliance — exactly the conditions that select for resistant survivors; finishing the full prescribed course helps prevent resistance.

examples.text: MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) survives drugs that once killed it, a resistance pattern driven by years of antibiotic exposure.

mcBank.stem: Which patient behavior most directly accelerates antimicrobial resistance?
options: Stopping antibiotics early after symptoms ease
Finishing the full prescribed course
Taking the drug at the prescribed dose
Reporting side effects to the nurse

mcBank.stem: One common molecular mechanism of antimicrobial resistance is
options: enzymes that chemically inactivate the drug
the microbe growing a thicker bone matrix
the host producing more histamine
the drug binding more tightly to its target

definition.text: Disease transmission is how pathogens move from a reservoir to new hosts — by direct or indirect contact, by living vectors, or through vehicles such as water, food, and air — a chain that infection control aims to break.

anchor.quote: Contact transmission includes direct contact or indirect contact

facts.text: Pathogens persist by living in reservoirs where they normally reside.

anchor.quote: they require reservoirs where they normally reside

facts.text: Indirect contact transmission spreads pathogens through contaminated inanimate objects called fomites.

anchor.quote: Indirect contact transmission involves inanimate objects called fomites that become contaminated by pathogens

facts.text: A vector is an animal, typically an arthropod, that carries a disease from one host to another.

anchor.quote: an animal (typically an arthropod) that carries the disease from one host to another

facts.text: Vehicle transmission spreads pathogens through water, food, and air.

anchor.quote: the transmission of pathogens through vehicles such as water, food, and air

misconceptions.text: Students assume that touching a contaminated object cannot spread infection unless the source person is present.
misconceptions.corrective: Indirect contact through fomites — doorknobs, bed rails, stethoscopes — transmits pathogens long after the source has gone, which is why surface disinfection and hand hygiene matter.

examples.text: Hand hygiene breaks the chain of infection by removing pathogens before a nurse's hands act as a fomite between patients.

mcBank.stem: A contaminated stethoscope that passes a pathogen between patients is an example of
options: indirect contact transmission via a fomite
vector transmission by an arthropod
vehicle transmission through air
direct person-to-person contact

mcBank.stem: A mosquito carrying a pathogen from one person to another is acting as a
options: vector
fomite
reservoir
vehicle

mapping.stages: reservoir, mode of transmission, susceptible host
mapping.dependency: a pathogen must leave a reservoir and travel a route before it can reach a new host
mapping.failure if skipped: breaking any link, such as hand hygiene removing the transmission route, stops the spread

attribution: OpenStax Microbiology, §16.3 Modes of Disease Transmission
